questions.text: An office building is NOT sprinklered. What is the maximum travel distance to an exit?

options.text: 30m (common misremembering—ERR-DSGN-020), which is often confused with other building types
45m unsprinklered; 60m if sprinklered (correct)
90m (overly conservative), typically used in larger, more complex buildings with advanced fire safety systems
Depends on building height; no fixed limit, though this is a misconception as limits are defined by code

rationale.a: Common error; under-estimates the actual limit.
rationale.d: Height does not affect travel distance limits; sprinkler status does.
rationale.correct: Unsprinklered = 45m max travel distance. Sprinklered = 60m (fire suppression allows longer travel). ERR-DSGN-020 documents the error of using 30m, which is too restrictive. NBC Chapter 4 mandates 45/60m per sprinkler status.

questions.text: A 3,000 sqm office floor has OL = 323 persons. Calculate required exits and minimum total exit width.

options.text: 2 exits, 1,616mm total (800mm each), which meets the minimum width requirements for safe evacuation
2 exits, 2,454mm total (1,227mm each, ensures 1,100mm minimum)
3 exits, 2,454mm total (818mm each—too narrow for compliance with safety standards)
2 exits, 2,600mm total (1,300mm each—oversized, providing additional safety margin)

rationale.a: Correct exits but under-calculates required width (1,616 ≠ 2,454).
rationale.c: Adds extra exit unnecessarily; OL 323 does not require 3 exits until OL > 500.
rationale.d: Slightly over-sized but functionally acceptable; 2,600mm for 2 exits = 1,300mm each.
rationale.correct: OL = 323 (50–499 range) → 2 exits. Required width = 323 × 7.6 = 2,454.8mm total. Distribute: 2,454 ÷ 2 = 1,227mm each. Minimum per exit = 1,100mm double leaf (or 900mm single leaf). 1,227mm exceeds both minimums ✓. Final design: 2 exits of 1,227mm each (or 2 exits of 1,300mm for round number).
rationale.takeaway: Exit count from OL range (50–499 → 2 exits). Exit width = OL × 7.6, distributed across required exits, each ≥ minimum (900mm or 1,100mm).

questions.text: A 5,000 sqm restaurant has 150 sqm kitchen and 4,850 sqm dining area. Calculate total occupant load and exits required. (Dining = 1.4 sqm/person, Kitchen = 9.3 sqm/person)

options.text: OL = 5,357 persons, 4 exits (grossly over-calculated, not feasible for the given space)
OL ≈ 3,571 persons, 4 exits (large restaurant, assuming maximum density without considering practical constraints)
OL ≈ 3,479 persons, 4 exits (150÷1.4 + 4,850÷9.3, correct loads)

rationale.a: Uses single factor (≈1.35) for entire space; ignores use-type differentiation.
rationale.b: Approximate value but calculation method not shown; likely using blended factor.
rationale.c: Uses dining factor for kitchen (9.3 vs 1.4 are not interchangeable); over-calculates OL.
rationale.d: Correct: separates by use type, applies correct factors.
rationale.correct: Kitchen: 150÷9.3 = 16 persons. Dining: 4,850÷1.4 = 3,464 persons. Total = 3,480 ≈ 3,479 (with rounding). OL 3,480 falls in 1,000+ range → 4 exits required. Using correct load factors by use type is critical.
rationale.takeaway: Always separate occupancy by use type. Kitchen ≠ dining area. Different load factors apply to each. Small miscalculation in load factor scales dramatically at large floor areas.

questions.text: An office floor is 50m × 50m (2,500 sqm). Exits are located only on one 50m side (North). If the building is sprinklered, can a person at the South side reach an exit within the travel distance limit?

options.text: Yes (South wall is 50m away; sprinklered max 60m, so 50m is within limit)
No (50m exceeds sprinklered limit of 45m, which is the standard for non-sprinklered buildings)
Yes, but only if exits are distributed; one-sided exits create dead-end corridors, which are not compliant with safety codes
No (offices require maximum 30m travel distance—ERR-DSGN-020, which is a common misconception)

rationale.c: Also correct; highlights that while travel distance is met, egress design should distribute exits to avoid dead-ends.
rationale.d: Uses wrong limit (30m—ERR-DSGN-020); correct sprinklered limit is 60m.
rationale.correct: South to North = 50m travel distance. Sprinklered building max = 60m. 50m < 60m ✓ travel distance is compliantOption 'c' correctly identifies the dead-end corridor violation created by one-sided exits exceeding dead-end limits, making 'a' incomplete. Travel distance alone does not override dead-end rules.South side (farthest point is ~50m away with only one direction of escape). Code may require distributed exits to avoid this dead-end condition, even if travel distance is within limit.
rationale.takeaway: Travel distance (50m < 60m) ✓; BUT if all exits are one-sided, dead-end corridor on far side may be a secondary issue. Distribute exits for redundancy.

questions.text: A classroom is 200 sqm with only 1 calculated exit. Why is 1 exit inadequate, and how many are actually required?

options.text: 1 exit is fine; 200 sqm ÷ 9.3 = 22 persons < 50 person limit, thus meeting the minimum requirement
1 exit is inadequate for classrooms; OL = 200÷2 = 100 persons → requires 2 exits (use correct load factor)
Classroom needs 2 exits minimum by code, regardless of OL, to ensure safe evacuation
Classroom load factor equals office (9.3); OL too low for 2 exits, but safety standards suggest otherwise

rationale.a: Uses wrong load factor (office instead of classroom); under-estimates OL.
rationale.c: Some codes do require 2 exits for classrooms as policy, but NBC calculates from occupancy load.
rationale.d: Repeats mistake of using office factor; classroom is denser (2.0 vs 9.3).
rationale.correct: Classroom load factor = 2.0 sqm/person (NOT office 9.3). OL = 200÷2 = 100 persons (50–499 range) → 2 exits required. Using office load factor (9.3) would give OL ≈ 22, incorrectly suggesting 1 exit. Many designs fail because they apply wrong load factors to specific use types.
rationale.takeaway: Always verify use type's load factor. Classroom (2.0) ≠ Office (9.3). Correct load factor directly affects exit count.

questions.text: What is the maximum length of a dead-end corridor in an unsprinklered building?

options.text: 4m (overly restrictive, often misunderstood in older codes)
6m unsprinklered; 12m sprinklered (correct)
10m (common error—ERR-DSGN-024, frequently cited in design reviews)
No limit on dead-ends; only total travel distance matters, which is a misconception in fire safety design

rationale.a: Too strict; 6m is the actual limit.
rationale.c: Common error; 10m exceeds the 6m unsprinklered limit.
rationale.d: Dead-end length is a separate check from total travel distance.
rationale.correct: Unsprinklered dead-end max = 6m (you can only escape one way). Sprinklered = 12m. ERR-DSGN-024 documents using 10m, which is incorrect. A dead-end is a corridor segment where you must backtrack to reach an exit (only one exit direction available).

questions.text: A 200 sqm office (business use) requires egress calculation. Calculate: (a) occupant load, (b) number of exits required, (c) total exit width needed.

options.text: (a) 22 persons, (b) 1 exit, (c) 168mm (too narrow) for compliance with standard egress requirements
(a) 21 persons, (b) 1 exit, (c) 160mm ≈159.6mm → must use 900mm minimum
(a) 43 persons, (b) 1 exit, (c) 327mm → must use 900mm minimum to ensure safe evacuation
(a) 50 persons, (b) 2 exits, (c) 380mm → 190mm each (too narrow) for the expected occupant load

rationale.a: Correct OL and exits, but says 168mm is the final answer—should note 900mm minimum applies.
rationale.c: Over-calculates OL (should be ~21, not 43); leads to 2 exits unnecessarily.
rationale.d: Over-calculates OL (should be 21, not 50); incorrect exit count and width.
rationale.correct: (a) OL = 200 sqm ÷ 9.3 sqm/person ≈21.5 → 21 persons. (b) OL < 50 → 1 exit required. (c) Required width = 21 × 7.6 = 159.6mm. BUT minimum exit door = 900mm, so actual exit width = 900mm (minimum takes precedence).
rationale.takeaway: Exit width = max(calculated width, 900mm minimum per exit). For small spaces, minimum governs.

questions.text: What is the correct exit width formula and the critical error in this field?

options.text: Exit width = OL × 5mm (simple, but ERR-DSGN-019 uses wrong factor)
Exit width = OL × 7.6mm (correct; ERR-DSGN-019 is using 5mm instead)
Exit width = OL × 10mm (conservative, safe choice)
Exit width = (OL ÷ 50) × 250mm (uses occupancy-based increments)

rationale.a: Identifies the error correctly but uses the wrong formula in the answer.
rationale.d: This is the stair width formula, not exit width.
rationale.correct: Exit width = OL × 7.6 mm/person (NOT 5mm). ERR-DSGN-019 documents the error of using 5mm, which under-sizes exits by ~33%. Example: 100 persons should get 760mm (minimum 900mm), but 5mm would give only 500mm—dangerously inadequate.
rationale.takeaway: ERR-DSGN-019: Exit width = OL × 7.6 mm/person (NOT 5mm). This is the highest-tested error in fire egress.

questions.text: A 400 sqm retail store (ground floor) has 2 exits of 900mm each. Is exit width adequate? (OL = 400÷2.8 ≈ 143 persons)

options.text: Yes (2 × 900 = 1,800mm ≥ 1,086mm required)
No (required 143 × 7.6 = 1,086mm → need exits >1,050mm each; 900mm is minimum)
No (900mm is too narrow for any retail; need 1,100mm minimum)
Yes (900mm × 2 meets code minimum; no extra width needed)

rationale.b: Calculation is correct but conclusion is wrong—1,800mm total ≥ 1,086mm required.
rationale.c: Confuses minimum (900mm door) with adequacy for load. 900mm is code minimum; total width governs.
rationale.d: Correct conclusion but reasoning is incomplete; should verify total width ≥ required width.
rationale.correct: OL = 400÷2.8 = 143 persons. Required width = 143×7.6 = 1,086.8mm total. Provided: 2×900 = 1,800mm total. Since 1,800 > 1,086, exit width is adequate ✓. Note: minimum per exit (900mm) is met, and total exceeds required (1,086mm).
rationale.takeaway: Exit width adequacy: total provided ≥ (OL × 7.6), AND each exit ≥ 900mm minimum. Both conditions must be met.

questions.text: A mixed-use building (ground: retail 200 sqm; upper: office 800 sqm) must calculate total occupant load and exits. Retail load factor = 2.8 sqm/person, office = 9.3 sqm/person. How many exits are required, and what is the minimum total exit width?

options.text: OL = 157 persons; 2 exits; 1,193mm total width required
OL = 200 persons; 2 exits; 1,520mm total width required
OL = 1,000 persons; 4 exits; 7,600mm total width required
OL = 300 persons; 2 exits; 2,280mm total width required

rationale.b: Over-counts occupancy; fails to differentiate load factors correctly.
rationale.c: Massively over-counts; uses wrong area or load factor for one category.
rationale.correct: Retail: 200÷2.8 = 71 persons. Office: 800÷9.3 = 86 persons. Total OL = 71 + 86 = 157 persons (50–499 range → 2 exits). Exit width = 157 × 7.6 = 1,193mm total. Distribute as ~600mm each (minimum 900mm per exit may apply, so actual provision could be 2×900mm = 1,800mm to meet both requirements).
rationale.takeaway: Always separate use types and apply correct load factors (retail 2.8, office 9.3, etc.). Sum OLs, determine exits from range, calculate required width = OL × 7.6, and verify each exit ≥ 900mm minimum.
